resolution.gpt_reasoning: Nevada’s nonpayment-of-rent eviction statute is NRS § 40.253, which requires a written notice demanding either payment of rent or surrender of the premises before the tenant is guilty of unlawful detainer for nonpayment. For residential premises, the current statutory period is 7 judicial days after service of the notice, not 5 days. The 5-day figure appears to reflect an outdated version or a different Nevada eviction notice, while the current nonpayment notice period is 7 judicial days under NRS § 40.253.
resolution.gemini_reasoning: Under NRS § 40.253(1), a tenant who defaults on rent is guilty of unlawful detainer only after being served with a written notice and continuing in possession for 7 judicial days. This statute was amended in 2019, changing the period from 5 days to 7 judicial days, which resolves the conflict between the sources; Source A is outdated, while Source B is correct.
resolution.uncertainty_note: The 7 days are judicial days, so weekends and legal holidays are generally excluded; special rules or additional notice requirements may apply for subsidized housing, lawful rent withholding under NRS § 118A.315, or other statutory exceptions.

flags.gpt_reasoning: Nevada residential pay-or-quit notices are served under NRS 40.280. Subsection (1)(a) covers personal delivery, subsection (1)(b) covers leaving the notice with a suitable person plus mailing, and subsection (1)(c) covers posting/other delivery when no suitable person or ascertainable address is available plus mailing; there is no mail-only method.
flags.gemini_reasoning: Nevada law specifies three methods for serving eviction notices under NRS 40.280(1). Subsection (a) covers personal delivery, (b) covers substituted service (leaving with a suitable person and mailing), and (c) covers posting the notice in a conspicuous place and mailing it when other methods are not possible. The 'current rules file' correctly identified all three valid service methods.

elements: Tenant engaged in protected activity (habitability complaint, union organizing, exercising legal rights)
Landlord knew of the protected activity
Adverse action (eviction, rent increase, service reduction) followed protected activity
Causal connection between protected activity and adverse action
Action was within state-defined presumption period (varies: 60 days to 12 months)
substantive_defenses.note: Anti-retaliation statute: NRS 118A.510. Presumption period, protected activities, and available remedies vary by state — attorney verification required. Statute identified via machine-assisted retrieval — attorney verification required before use

elements: Tenant is member of a protected class (race, color, national origin, sex, disability, familial status, religion — per federal FHA; state law may add classes)
Similarly situated non-protected tenants were treated more favorably, OR discriminatory intent can be shown, OR facially neutral policy has disparate impact
substantive_defenses.note: Federal FHA prohibits discrimination in housing based on protected class. State law may provide additional protected classes and remedies. Discriminatory intent or disparate impact analysis is fact-intensive — specialist review required. grounding_gap: state fair housing case law and protected class details.

elements: Tenant had a valid lease or tenancy
Landlord substantially interfered with tenant's right to peaceful possession
substantive_defenses.note: Breach of covenant of quiet enjoyment — primarily common law doctrine in most states; some states codify at RLTA. grounding_gap: whether state recognizes as affirmative defense to eviction, constructive eviction standard, and remedies vary — specialist review required.

elements: Amount demanded in notice exceeds lawfully owed rent
Impermissible charges included (late fees, utilities, damages, other non-rent items)
substantive_defenses.note: Improper rent calculation — relevant where landlord has included improper charges (late fees, fees not authorized by lease) in the rent demand. grounding_gap: state-specific rules on what may be included in rent demand, and whether overcharge voids notice — specialist review required.
